Landowners Must Receive Surface Water Flowing Naturally From Higher Ground
An important principle of Illinois drainage law is that the owner of servient land must receive the water that flows naturally onto his land. The law further implies that an embankment constructed across a natural water-course must be built with enough openings to take care of water that would flow across the right of way in a state of nature.
In litigation the first point often in question is whether the location where the surface water is discharged is considered a natural watercourse. It is important in analyzing problems of this type to distinguish between natural and artificial watercourses to determine limitations on what can be done in such areas as obstruction, maintenance, etc.
3. Improvements Made To Natural Watercourses
Natural watercourses periodically require maintenance and improvements. A natural watercourse is not required to be used only in its natural state, but may be improved either by being deepened or widened by artificial means or by the construction of a drain along the course of its channel to more effectively carry the surface water off the land. The construction of such an improvement is not considered as a creation of a new watercourse nor is it considered as an abandonment of the natural watercourse.
4. Drainage Rights Within Boundaries of Individual Owner
Artificial watercourses may be constructed by individual or public landowners, including the Division, and the direction of natural flow may be changed within the boundaries of their property in the absence of any contractual or prescriptive right provided (a) an added burden is not imposed on the property of another, and (b) the water is restored to its natural or original channel before it leaves the property.
